ST JAMES'S HOSPITAL
CARDIOLOGY DEPARTMENT

Patient Name: Mr David Griffiths
DOB: 12/05/1974
NHS Number: 123 456 7890
Consultant: Dr A. Sharma
Date of MDT: 15/11/2023

Dear Dr Patel,

RE: Mr David Griffiths

We reviewed this 49-year-old gentleman in the cardiology multi-disciplinary meeting today regarding his symptomatic ventricular ectopy. 

Mr Griffiths presented three months ago with palpitations and occasional lightheadedness. Initial assessment revealed frequent ventricular ectopic beats on 24-hour Holter monitoring (burden 8%). Echocardiography demonstrated structurally normal heart with preserved left ventricular function (LVEF 58%), normal valves, and no regional wall motion abnormalities. He has no history of syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, or structural heart disease.

Following our previous consultation, Mr Griffiths was commenced on bisoprolol 2.5mg once daily. He reports excellent symptom control with this medication and has had no further significant palpitations or lightheadedness. He has tolerated the medication well with no side effects. Follow-up Holter monitoring two weeks ago shows significant reduction in ventricular ectopic burden to 2%, with no complex ventricular arrhythmias noted.

Mr Griffiths understands his condition and the plan for ongoing management. He is aware of when to seek medical attention should symptoms recur. He feels confident in managing his condition with current medication.

MDT CONCLUSIONS:
1. Symptomatic ventricular ectopy in structurally normal heart
2. Excellent response to beta-blocker therapy with good symptom control
3. Stable condition with no concerning features
4. No indication for electrophysiological study at present
5. Medications optimised - bisoprolol 2.5mg once daily

PLAN:
We recommend placing Mr Griffiths on a continuous Patient Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) pathway. He should continue bisoprolol 2.5mg once daily and contact the cardiology department directly if symptoms recur or worsen. No routine follow-up appointments are required.

We will copy this letter to Mr Griffiths for his records.

Yours sincerely,

Dr A. Sharma
Consultant Cardiologist

Dear GP,

RE: MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAM MEETING - VALVULAR HEART DISEASE CLINIC

Thank you for referring Mrs Wilson to our Valvular Heart Disease MDT clinic.

Clinical History:
Mrs Wilson was referred with a heart murmur detected at routine GP check. She reports no cardiac symptoms and remains fully active, participating in regular swimming and walking without limitation. There is no history of palpitations, syncope, chest pain, or breathlessness. She has a history of well-controlled hypertension for 5 years.

Investigations:
Recent echocardiogram (12/03/2024):
- Mitral valve shows bileaflet prolapse with mild to moderate mitral regurgitation (MR)
- Regurgitant volume: 35ml/beat
- Effective regurgitant orifice area: 0.25cm²
- Vena contracta width: 4.5mm
- No leaflet thickening or calcification
- Left ventricular size and function normal (LVEF 58%)
- Left atrium mildly dilated (38ml/m²)
- Right heart chambers normal
- No other valvular abnormalities

Resting ECG (12/03/2024): Normal sinus rhythm, normal axis, no conduction abnormalities.

Medications:
- Ramipril 5mg OD (stable dose for 2 years)
- Simvastatin 20mg ON
- No anticoagulation required

MDT Discussion (14/03/2024):
The MDT reviewed Mrs Wilson's case. There is consensus that this represents non-severe mitral valve prolapse with mild to moderate MR. She remains entirely asymptomatic with normal left ventricular function. No indication for surgical intervention at present.

Plan:
1. Mrs Wilson has been fully educated about her condition and when to seek medical attention if symptoms develop (breathlessness, palpitations, reduced exercise tolerance).
2. We recommend a Patient Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) pathway with her current medications continued.
3. Surveillance echocardiogram arranged for 2 years' time (March 2026) to monitor valve progression.
4. Mrs Wilson understands she should contact the valve clinic directly if she develops any cardiac symptoms between now and her next scheduled scan.
5. Discharge letter sent to patient with PIFU information leaflet and contact details.

Mrs Wilson was seen in clinic today, is comfortable with this management plan, and has consented to PIFU pathway.

Please continue current medications and manage hypertension as per usual. We will review the echocardiogram results in 2026 and contact you if any concerning changes are noted.

Yours sincerely,

Dr A. Chambers

To: Dr M Khan, GP Surgery, 23 High Street, Birmingham B15 2AB
From: Dr S Rajan, Consultant Cardiologist, Heart Failure Service, University Hospitals Birmingham
Date: 15/11/2024
Re: Mr Peter Wilkinson (DOB: 12/08/1959) NHS: 785 463 8912

Dear Dr Khan,

Thank you for referring Mr Wilkinson to our heart failure clinic. He attended today with his wife for review.

Mr Wilkinson is a 65-year-old gentleman with a history of heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction (HFmrEF), diagnosed six months ago following an admission with acute decompensated heart failure. His recent echocardiogram (05/10/2024) shows an ejection fraction of 43% (improved from 35% at diagnosis), mild-moderate mitral regurgitation, and mild left atrial enlargement. His BNP from last week remains elevated at 350 ng/L (previously 420 ng/L).

Clinically, he reports worsening symptoms over the last four weeks. He was previously NYHA class II but now describes consistent breathlessness on minimal exertion (walking 20 metres on the flat), equivalent to NYHA class III. He has had two episodes of waking at night short of breath in the last fortnight and reports increased ankle swelling despite good adherence to his fluid restriction (1.5L/day). His weight has increased by 2.5 kg over the last month.

His current medications are:
- Bisoprolol 5mg OD (up-titrated one month ago)
- Ramipril 5mg BD
- Spironolactone 25mg OD
- Furosemide 40mg OD (increased from 20mg two weeks ago)

He is tolerating these doses, but his symptoms are clearly not controlled. We have not yet achieved optimal guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for his HFmrEF, as further up-titration of his ACE-inhibitor and beta-blocker is needed, but is currently limited by his borderline blood pressure (105/65 mmHg today) and symptomatic burden.

PLAN:
1. We have increased his furosemide to 40mg BD for the next two weeks to try and achieve better euvolaemia.
2. He will have repeat bloods (U&E, BNP) in one week via his GP.
3. We have arranged a follow-up appointment in our specialist heart failure clinic in 4 weeks (12/12/2024) to re-assess his clinical status, review bloods, and attempt further medication optimisation.
4. We have reinforced the HF traffic light advice and asked him to contact the heart failure nurse helpline if his symptoms worsen further (red zone).

Given his uncontrolled and worsening symptoms, ongoing need for medication optimisation, and recent clinical decompensation (symptomatic deterioration), he is not suitable for patient-initiated follow-up (PIFU) at this time. He requires regular specialist review until his condition is stabilised.

Yours sincerely,

Dr S Rajan
Consultant Cardiologist

Coronary angiography performed last month revealed no significant coronary artery disease, confirming an idiopathic VT substrate.

**CLINICAL ASSESSMENT:**
Today, Mr Henderson reports feeling 'much better' with no further syncope. He describes occasional palpitations but these are brief and not debilitating. He was started on bisoprolol 5mg once daily two months ago. I have increased this today to 7.5mg once daily. We discussed the option of a flecainide trial but have deferred this decision. He tolerates bisoprolol well with no side effects.

1. Continue bisoprolol 7.5mg once daily. We will review his response to this dose increase.
2. I have arranged a repeat 48-hour Holter monitor in 6 weeks (end of April 2024) to assess VT burden on the higher beta-blocker dose.

Dear Dr Singh,

RE: Thomas Richardson - MDT discussion regarding paroxysmal atrial fibrillation

Thank you for referring Mr Richardson. He was discussed at the cardiology MDT meeting on 12/03/2025.

CLINICAL SUMMARY:
Mr Richardson is a 67-year-old gentleman with a 2-year history of symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF). He reports episodes lasting 4-6 hours approximately every 4-6 weeks, characterised by palpitations, mild shortness of breath, and fatigue. He has no structural heart disease confirmed by echocardiogram 18 months ago showing normal LV function (EF 55-60%) and normal valves.

MEDICATIONS:
- Bisoprolol 5mg OD (recently increased from 2.5mg OD)
- Apixaban 5mg BD
- Atorvastatin 40mg ON

The MDT noted that his rhythm control therapy may not be fully optimised. The bisoprolol was increased just 3 weeks ago to improve rate control during episodes, but we have not yet seen him for reassessment since this change. Symptoms persist but are described as "moderately bothersome" rather than severe.

He remains NYHA Class I-II with preserved exercise tolerance between episodes. No hospital admissions in the last 12 months. Recent blood tests show normal renal function, electrolytes, and thyroid function.

MDT DISCUSSION:
The team discussed whether to proceed with catheter ablation versus continued medical management. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3 (age, hypertension, male), with HAS-BLED score of 1. There is equipoise regarding the next step - he meets criteria for ablation given symptomatic episodes despite beta-blocker therapy, but we have not yet had his formal response to the recent medication optimisation.

We also discussed that he has a history of mild anxiety and occasional medication adherence issues, which may affect his ability to reliably monitor symptoms and initiate contact if needed.

RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Arrange clinical review in 3 months to assess response to increased bisoprolol dose
2. Consider repeat 24-hour Holter monitoring to quantify AF burden
3. Discuss ablation options with patient at next consultation
4. Ensure he has clear written information about when to contact the arrhythmia nurse specialist
5. Follow-up plan remains uncertain pending assessment of medication optimisation and patient preference regarding invasive treatment

Yours sincerely,

Dr Helen Carter

Mr. Richardson has a history of persistent atrial fibrillation diagnosed in August 2022. He also has symptomatic ventricular ectopy with frequent premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) on recent ambulatory monitoring (PVC burden 12%). His comorbidities include essential hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, both well-controlled.

He remains symptomatic with intermittent palpitations and occasional dizzy spells, despite optimisation of his rhythm control strategy. He is currently maintained on flecainide 100mg BD for his persistent AF, having failed rate control with beta-blockers due to intolerable fatigue. I will need to keep him under long-term follow-up in our cardiology clinic to monitor his response to treatment, reassess his symptoms, and plan for potential invasive interventions.

Medication Plan:
- Continue flecainide 100mg BD
- Continue aspirin 75mg OD
- Continue atorvastatin 40mg ON
- Continue ramipril 5mg OD

We will arrange for Mr. Richardson to be seen again in our outpatient clinic in 4 months to review his symptoms and discuss therapeutic options further. GP: Dr. S. Miller

Dear Dr. Miller,

RE: Mr. David CHEN
DOB: 05/11/1985
NHS No: 123 456 7890

Thank you for referring this 39-year-old gentleman who was admitted following an episode of pre-excited atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.

He presented with a 45-minute episode of sudden-onset palpitations, dizziness and chest discomfort. His ECG on arrival showed pre-excited atrial fibrillation with a wide-complex irregular tachycardia at 220 beats per minute. This converted spontaneously to sinus rhythm during transfer to the Cardiac Monitoring Unit, revealing a short PR interval with delta waves in leads II, III, aVF, and V4-V6 consistent with a left posteroseptal accessory pathway.

Mr. Chen reports 3 similar but shorter episodes over the past 18 months, all self-terminating within 10-15 minutes. He describes them as 'alarming but manageable' and denies syncope or presyncope beyond the initial dizziness. He has no significant cardiac history and is otherwise well with normal exercise tolerance. There is no family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy.

An echocardiogram performed during admission shows structurally normal heart with preserved left ventricular function (ejection fraction 58%). There was no evidence of Ebstein anomaly or other congenital abnormalities.

We have commenced oral bisoprolol 2.5mg once daily for symptom control. He has been counselled on the Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome diagnosis and the associated small lifetime risk of sudden cardiac death (approximately 1 in 1000). Electrophysiological study with possible catheter ablation was discussed as the definitive curative option. However, given the intermittent nature of his symptoms and his preference to avoid invasive procedures at this stage, we have agreed on a trial of medical management.

We plan to review him in the cardiology clinic in 8 weeks to assess symptom control and tolerance of medication. His understanding of when to seek urgent medical attention (prolonged palpitations >30 minutes, syncope, chest pain) appears satisfactory. We have asked him to keep a symptom diary.

He is being discharged today with:
1. Bisoprolol 2.5mg once daily
2. Advice sheet on Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
3. Cardiology follow-up appointment to be sent

Yours sincerely,

Dr. Aisha Khan
Consultant Cardiologist
St. Mary's University Hospital

A comprehensive echocardiogram at that time showed preserved left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 55%) with evidence of diastolic dysfunction and left atrial enlargement.

Investigations: Recent blood tests show NT-proBNP 220 ng/L (down from 480 ng/L at diagnosis). Renal function and electrolytes within normal limits.

Current medication:

Medication review: All heart failure medications have been optimised according to guidelines. Mrs Johnson tolerates them well with no significant side effects.

He reports being able to undertake usual daily activities without limitation. An ECG performed two weeks ago showed sinus rhythm with no ectopy. - Persistent AF status post-ablation
- Last echocardiogram six months ago showed preserved LV function (EF 55%)
- Occasional mild symptoms reported
- No recent hospital admissions
- Medications: apixaban only (anticoagulation optimised)
- Rate control medications discontinued
- Patient expresses preference for self-management

MDT DISCUSSION
The team noted that while Mr Wilkinson appears clinically stable and symptomatically improved post-ablation, several factors warrant caution. Persistent AF with ablation typically requires careful monitoring of LV function post-procedure. The documentation does not contain a recent assessment of LV function (no echo within last 3-6 months), and his age is not documented which is relevant for risk stratification. Additionally, there is mention of occasional symptoms which may indicate incomplete rhythm control.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Arrange repeat echocardiogram to assess current LV function
2. Consider 24-hour Holter monitoring to evaluate rhythm control
3. Document patient's age formally in records
4. Review in clinic in 3 months to reassess stability before considering PIFU pathway
5. Continue apixaban as per current prescription

A subsequent flecainide challenge confirmed the diagnosis of Brugada Syndrome. He has no structural heart disease, with a recent echocardiogram showing a structurally normal heart with preserved left ventricular function (ejection fraction 65%). He has been educated on lifestyle modifications (avoiding fevers, certain medications, excessive alcohol) and has an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in situ, implanted three months ago for primary prevention, which is functioning well on device check.

Given his diagnosis of an inherited channelopathy (Brugada Syndrome), his management requires lifelong specialist oversight within the inherited cardiac conditions (ICC) service. His condition, while stable on current therapy, carries a lifelong risk of malignant arrhythmias and requires periodic review of ICD programming, genetic counselling for his family, and potential adjustments to therapy based on emerging evidence. His care cannot be safely transferred to primary care.

BACKGROUND:
Mr Khan presented with recurrent episodes of palpitations associated with dizziness. A resting ECG showed evidence of pre-excitation with a short PR interval and delta waves. Holter monitoring demonstrated intermittent pre-excitation with no sustained arrhythmias. Echocardiogram performed six months ago was reported as normal left ventricular function (EF 60%) with no structural abnormalities. He was previously started on bisoprolol 2.5mg once daily which he reports has reduced symptom frequency but not eliminated episodes entirely.

MDT DISCUSSION:
The team reviewed the clinical history, ECG findings, and previous investigations. There was consensus that this represents an accessory pathway with intermittent conduction. The current medical management with beta-blocker has provided partial symptom control, but breakthrough episodes continue to occur approximately monthly.

KEY CONSIDERATIONS:
1. The patient reports ongoing symptoms despite medical therapy
2. The pathway appears to be intermittent rather than persistent
3. Age is not documented in the referral information, though the patient appears to be an adult
4. The echocardiogram shows preserved LV function with no structural heart disease
5. There is uncertainty regarding the precise risk stratification for this accessory pathway

RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. The team feels further risk stratification is required before determining optimal management pathway
2. Consideration of an exercise stress test to assess persistence of pre-excitation at higher heart rates
3. Potential need for electrophysiological study for definitive pathway localization and risk assessment
4. If non-invasive risk stratification is reassuring, transition to PIFU with symptom-triggered follow-up could be considered
5. Current medication should be continued pending further investigations

NEXT STEPS:
Please arrange exercise stress testing and consider referral for electrophysiological study. The patient should continue current medication and report any worsening symptoms. A further MDT review will be scheduled once these investigations are complete to determine definitive management.

Yours sincerely,

Dear Dr Reynolds,

**MDT DISCUSSION (11/11/2024):** Ms Carter's case was reviewed by the Cardiology Multidisciplinary Team for her known aortic valve disease. The team had access to her recent echocardiogram report from 05/10/2024 and her clinic notes from your referral. A decision regarding the most appropriate follow-up pathway was discussed.

**CLINICAL SUMMARY:** Ms Carter has known moderate aortic regurgitation (AR), first diagnosed in 2020. She has remained largely asymptomatic but reported a single episode of mild exertional dyspnoea on walking uphill three weeks ago, which resolved spontaneously. She denies chest pain, syncope, or ankle swelling. Her current medications are Bisoprolol 2.5mg OD and Ramipril 2.5mg OD for well-controlled hypertension. Blood pressure today was 135/85 mmHg.

**ECHOCARDIOGRAM (05/10/2024) FINDINGS:**
- Moderate aortic regurgitation with vena contracta 4-5mm. Regurgitant volume appears significant but quantification was technically difficult.
- Aortic root size is 38mm.
- **Left Ventricular Function: Left ventricular size is mildly dilated (LV end-diastolic dimension 56mm). Ejection fraction is reported as 'low normal' (estimated 50-52%), but visual assessment suggested borderline function. No wall motion abnormalities noted.**
- Right ventricle normal.

**MDT CONSENSUS:** The MDT noted the patient's long-standing, largely stable valvular disease. The recent, isolated episode of dyspnoea, while mild, is a new symptom. The main areas of uncertainty were:
1.  **Symptomatic Status:** Is the reported dyspnoea a true indicator of progression?
2.  **Condition Severity:** The regurgitation is labelled 'moderate' but with 'significant' haemodynamics, bordering on moderate-to-severe classification.
3.  **Left Ventricular Status:** The LV function is described with conflicting terms ('low normal EF 50-52%' vs. 'borderline function'), and the presence of mild LV dilation is noted. It is unclear if this represents stable, adaptive remodelling or early ventricular impairment.

Given these uncertainties, the MDT did not feel confident in finalising a follow-up plan today.

**DECISION:** We recommend a **clinician-led review** of Ms Carter to formally reassess her symptomatic status, perform a detailed clinical examination, and clarify the echocardiographic findings. The need for further imaging (e.g., cardiac MRI for precise quantification and LV function) will be considered at that appointment. Pending this review, she should **not** be placed on a standard PIFU pathway.

We will contact Ms Carter to arrange this clinical review. If she develops worsening symptoms in the interim, please advise her to contact the surgery or our Cardiology Helpline as per the advice leaflet she will receive.

Thank you for referring Mrs Wilson to our Heart Valve MDT for review. The MDT meeting was held on 18/03/2025 with input from our Consultant Cardiologists, Cardiac Surgeons, and Echocardiography team.

**Clinical History:** Mrs Wilson is a 67-year-old lady who presented with progressive shortness of breath on exertion (NYHA Class III) over the last six months. She reports reduced exercise tolerance, now limited to walking 100 yards on flat ground. She has a background of treated hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

**Key Findings:**
- **Trans thoracic Echocardiogram (05/03/2025):** Shows severe calcific aortic stenosis. Peak velocity 4.4 m/s, mean gradient 45 mmHg. Aortic valve area calculated at 0.9 cm².

Mrs Wilson has **severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with concomitant left ventricular systolic dysfunction** (Stage D2 disease according to ESC guidelines).

Thank you for referring this 68-year-old lady under our care. I saw Ms Thompson today for a routine follow-up appointment following her transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, which she underwent 8 months ago on 15/07/2023.

**Current Clinical Status:**

She can now walk 20-30 minutes on the flat without stopping, compared to being housebound pre-procedure. She does, however, describe intermittent fatigue and occasional shortness of breath when climbing more than one flight of stairs, which she attributes to her age.

A surveillance transthoracic echocardiogram was performed one month ago (14/02/2024). The bioprosthetic aortic valve appears normally seated and functioning well. Ms Thompson's TAVI valve is functioning well, and she has derived significant symptomatic benefit. Her medications are optimised, and she has had no unplanned admissions since the procedure.

The plan today was to consider discharge to a Patient Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) pathway. However, there are a few areas of uncertainty that require clinical discretion before a final decision is made.

**REASON FOR MDT:** Review of ventricular tachycardia (VT) in setting of known ischaemic cardiomyopathy for management planning.

**CLINICAL SUMMARY:**
Mr Roberts is a 58-year-old gentleman with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy secondary to myocardial infarction in 2020. His most recent echocardiogram (09/01/2024) shows a severely impaired left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 28% (severe). He was admitted 3 months ago (December 2023) with an episode of sustained monomorphic VT, requiring electrical cardioversion. **DISCUSSION:**
The MDT reviewed the complex nature of his arrhythmia in the context of significant structural heart disease. His VT is clearly secondary to his ischaemic cardiomyopathy with scar-related substrate. Although his medication has been optimised for his heart failure, his recent admission for VT and ongoing symptomatic burden make his condition unstable for a self-managed pathway. **Dear Dr Sharma,**

**Re: Discharge from Cardiology Outpatient Clinic**

I am writing to inform you that Mrs Henderson has been discharged from the cardiology outpatient clinic following her review today. She will be transitioned to a Patient Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) pathway for the management of her stable heart failure.

**Background:** Mrs Henderson has a known history of ischaemic cardiomyopathy and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), diagnosed in 2021 following an anterior STEMI. She underwent primary PCI with DES to the LAD. Her last echocardiogram in October 2023 showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 42%, an improvement from 35% in 2022. She has been under regular cardiology follow-up.

**Recent Assessment:** Today, Mrs Henderson reports feeling very well. She is managing all her usual activities, including gardening and walking her dog for 30 minutes daily without breathlessness or undue fatigue. She has had no symptoms of orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea for over a year. She has had no hospital admissions since 2022 and no episodes of decompensation in the last 18 months. Her weight is stable, and she monitors it weekly. She confirms a good understanding of her 'traffic light' HF self-management plan.

**Medication Review:** Her guideline-directed medical therapy is fully optimised and has been stable for 12 months: Bisoprolol 7.5mg OD, Ramipril 10mg OD, Spironolactone 25mg OD, Dapagliflozin 10mg OD, and Furosemide 40mg OD PRN. She tolerates these well with no significant side effects. Recent bloods (12/03/2024) show stable renal function (eGFR 68 ml/min) and electrolytes. NT-proBNP is 180 ng/L (down from 450 ng/L a year ago).

**Plan:**
1.  **Discharge to PIFU Pathway:** Mrs Henderson's HF is clinically stable with optimised therapy. She and her husband understand the PIFU process and the 'amber/red flag' system for contacting the heart failure nurse helpline. We have provided her with the contact details and a written management plan.
2.  **Surveillance:** I have requested a routine surveillance echocardiogram in 2 years' time (by April 2026). The results will be reviewed remotely; she will only be recalled if there is a significant change.

Thank you for your ongoing care of this patient. Please do not hesitate to contact the Heart Failure Nurse Specialist team if you have any concerns.

Yours sincerely,

Dear Dr Patel,

Re: Mrs Eleanor Roberts, DOB 05/08/1949

Thank you for referring Mrs Roberts to our service. Her case was reviewed in the Valve MDT meeting today. We discussed her recent percutaneous mitral valve edge-to-edge repair (TEER) performed on 15/11/2024 for significant functional mitral regurgitation (MR).

**Clinical Summary:**
Mrs Roberts is a 75-year-old lady with a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation (rate-controlled on bisoprolol 2.5mg od and apixaban 5mg bd). She underwent a successful TEER procedure four months ago for symptomatic severe functional MR (NYHA III) secondary to left ventricular dysfunction (baseline LVEF 40%).

**Follow-up Investigations:**
1. **Recent Transthoracic Echo (10/03/2025):** Shows a well-seated TEER device with no significant residual mitral regurgitation (now graded as mild). The left ventricle is mildly dilated with mild global hypokinesia. The left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is 45%, showing improvement from her baseline. Left atrium is moderately dilated. No other significant valve abnormalities.
2. **ECG (10/03/2025):** Shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate of 68 bpm.
3. **Bloods (10/03/2025):** U&E, LFT, FBC are within normal ranges. NT-proBNP is 450 ng/L (down from 1200 ng/L pre-procedure).

**Current Status:**
Mrs Roberts reports feeling very well, with no breathlessness, chest pain, or oedema. She is managing all her usual daily activities and walks her dog for 30 minutes daily without symptoms (now NYHA I). Her medications are optimised and stable: bisoprolol 2.5mg od, apixaban 5mg bd, ramipril 5mg od, atorvastatin 40mg nocte. She has a good understanding of her condition and knows to contact the valve clinic if she develops worsening breathlessness, dizziness, or leg swelling.

**MDT Decision and Plan:**
The MDT agrees Mrs Roberts has made an excellent recovery post-TEER. Her mitral valve disease is now moderate (mild residual MR) with preserved LV function and she is entirely asymptomatic. All investigations are satisfactory and medications are optimal. There are no outstanding procedures or investigations planned.

**We therefore recommend:**
1. Mrs Roberts is suitable for a **Patient Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) pathway**.
2. She will be placed on a **timed PIFU pathway with a 2-year review window**, aligned with her next routine surveillance echocardiogram.
3. She has been provided with written and verbal information on the PIFU pathway, including clear instructions on symptoms that should prompt contact.
4. Please continue her current medication regimen.
5. We will write to her confirming these arrangements.

**Next Steps:**
A routine surveillance echocardiogram will be arranged for approximately March 2027 (2 years). Mrs Roberts understands she should contact the Valve Clinic Nurse Specialist if she experiences any concerning symptoms before then.

Thank you for your ongoing care of this patient.

Yours sincerely,

Dr S. Thompson

Thank you for referring this 56-year-old lady with symptoms of palpitations and occasional lightheadedness.

**History:** Mrs Sullivan has been experiencing intermittent palpitations for approximately 9 months, described as 'fluttering' or 'missed beats' in her chest, sometimes associated with brief lightheadedness. She reports no syncope, chest pain, or significant dyspnoea. She is otherwise well, with no significant past medical history. Family history is unremarkable for sudden cardiac death.

**Investigations:** Recent ambulatory ECG monitoring (14-day Zio patch, completed 30/01/2024) showed frequent monomorphic ventricular ectopy, with an average burden of 8%. There were no sustained ventricular arrhythmias. 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with occasional ventricular ectopic beats, QTc 430ms. Echocardiogram (05/01/2024) reports normal left ventricular size and function (EF 60%), no structural abnormalities, and normal valves.

**Assessment:** Symptomatic ventricular ectopy in a structurally normal heart. The ectopic burden is moderate and likely accounts for her symptoms.

**Management:** We discussed treatment options including reassurance, beta-blocker therapy, or possible electrophysiology study and ablation. Mrs Sullivan is keen to avoid invasive procedures if possible. We have initiated bisoprolol 1.25mg once daily today, a very low dose, with a plan to up-titrate based on symptom response and tolerance.

**Plan:**
- Continue bisoprolol 1.25mg OD. Please review in 2 weeks and consider increasing to 2.5mg OD if symptoms persist and she tolerates the medication well.
- We have provided patient information on ventricular ectopy and when to seek help.
- Arrange a follow-up 24-hour Holter monitor in 3 months to reassess ectopic burden once medication is optimised.
- Mrs Sullivan has been advised to contact the Arrhythmia Nurse Specialist via our PIFU line if symptoms worsen or if she experiences any concerning symptoms such as syncope or severe dizziness.

Given that medication optimisation is in its early stages and we need to assess her response to therapy, I have placed her on a **Patient Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) pathway for now, but this requires clinician confirmation** once her treatment is stabilised. The final decision regarding long-term PIFU suitability will depend on her symptom control with optimal medical therapy.

Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any concerns.

Yours sincerely,

Dr A. Khan
Consultant Cardiologist & Electrophysiologist

**RE: Mr Stephen Anderson**

Thank you for referring this 58-year-old gentleman who presented for routine follow-up of known aortic regurgitation.

**History:**
Mr Anderson was diagnosed with moderate aortic regurgitation in 2021 following an echocardiogram for a murmur. He has been followed up annually since with echocardiography and clinical review. He remains asymptomatic with good exercise tolerance (NYHA Class I). He leads an active lifestyle, walking 3 miles daily without symptoms.

**Examination:**
He is well appearing with BMI 24. Heart rate 72 bpm regular, BP 128/74 mmHg. Soft ejection systolic murmur and early diastolic murmur heard best at left sternal edge. No signs of heart failure.

**Investigations:**
Recent echocardiogram (20/03/2024) shows:
- Moderate aortic regurgitation (vena contracta 4.2 mm, regurgitant volume 45 mL)
- Normal left ventricular size and function (LVEDD 52 mm, LVEF 58%)
- No evidence of progressive aortic root dilation (aortic root 38 mm)
- Normal diastolic function

ECG shows sinus rhythm with no significant abnormalities. Recent blood tests show normal renal function and electrolytes.

**Management:**
No specific medication required. Blood pressure remains well controlled. No indication for surgical intervention at present.

**Assessment:**
This gentleman has stable moderate aortic regurgitation with preserved left ventricular function and no symptoms. His condition has remained unchanged over three years of surveillance.

**Plan:**
I have discussed options for follow-up with Mr Anderson, who understands his condition well. Given his stability, he is suitable for Patient-Initiated Follow-Up (PIFU) with our cardiology service.

**PIFU Pathway:** Continuous PIFU with scheduled surveillance echocardiography every 2 years (next echo due March 2026). He will self-manage between imaging episodes and contact the valve surveillance helpline if he develops new symptoms (dyspnoea, chest pain, palpitations, or reduced exercise tolerance). Results will be reviewed by a specialist, and he will only be recalled if there is significant change.

I have provided him with written information about the PIFU pathway and symptom management advice.

Please continue his usual cardiovascular care. I will remain available for PIFU contacts and will review his next surveillance echo results.
